claim: The acrosome is a membranous organelle positioned in the anterior portion of the sperm head and is essential for male fertility.
source: The acrosome is a membranous organelle positioned in the anterior portion of the sperm head and is essential for male fertility.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Acrosome biogenesis requires the dynamic cytoskeletal shuttling of vesicles toward nascent acrosome which is regulated by a series of accessory proteins.
source: Acrosome biogenesis requires the dynamic cytoskeletal shuttling of vesicles toward nascent acrosome which is regulated by a series of accessory proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: SSH2 is essential for acrosome biogenesis and male fertility.
source: Here, we generated Ssh2 knockout (KO) mice and HA-tagged Ssh2 knock-in (KI) mice to define the functions of Slingshot phosphatase 2 (SSH2) in spermatogenesis and demonstrated that as a regulator of actin remodeling, SSH2 is essential for acrosome biogenesis and male fertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Ssh2 KO and KI mice generated in this study.

claim: In Ssh2 KO males, spermatogenesis was arrested at the early spermatid stage with increased apoptotic index.
source: In Ssh2 KO males, spermatogenesis was arrested at the early spermatid stage with increased apoptotic index and the impaired acrosome biogenesis was characterized by defective transport/fusion of proacrosomal vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in Ssh2 KO mice as described in the abstract.

claim: Impaired acrosome biogenesis in Ssh2 KO males was characterized by defective transport/fusion of proacrosomal vesicles.
source: In Ssh2 KO males, spermatogenesis was arrested at the early spermatid stage with increased apoptotic index and the impaired acrosome biogenesis was characterized by defective transport/fusion of proacrosomal vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in Ssh2 KO mice.

claim: Disorganized F-actin structures accompanied by excessive phosphorylation of COFILIN were observed in the testes of Ssh2 KO mice.
source: Moreover, disorganized F-actin structures accompanied by excessive phosphorylation of COFILIN were observed in the testes of Ssh2 KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in Ssh2 KO mice.

claim: SSH2 has a modulatory role in acrosome biogenesis through COFILIN-mediated actin remodeling.
source: Collectively, our data reveal a modulatory role for SSH2 in acrosome biogenesis through COFILIN-mediated actin remodeling and the indispensability of this phosphatase in male fertility in mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: SSH2 is indispensable for male fertility in mice.
source: Collectively, our data reveal a modulatory role for SSH2 in acrosome biogenesis through COFILIN-mediated actin remodeling and the indispensability of this phosphatase in male fertility in mice.
evidence: This is supported by the complete infertility observed in Ssh2 KO males.

claim: Impaired spermatogenesis is the most common cause of non-obstructive azoospermia.
source: The most common cause of non-obstructive azoospermia is impaired spermatogenesis (i.e., the production of mature spermatozoa), which is behind about 15% of infertility cases in men (Agarwal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Agarwal et al., 2021.

claim: Impaired spermatogenesis is behind about 15% of infertility cases in men.
source: The most common cause of non-obstructive azoospermia is impaired spermatogenesis (i.e., the production of mature spermatozoa), which is behind about 15% of infertility cases in men (Agarwal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Agarwal et al., 2021.

claim: In mice, spermatogenesis is routinely subdivided into 12 stages of developmental progression.
source: In basic studies of mice, spermatogenesis—a continuous course to generate spermatozoa within the seminiferous epithelia incorporating the mitosis of undifferentiated spermatogonia, meiosis of spermatocytes, and eventually spermatid cytodifferentiation—is routinely subdivided into 12 stages of developmental progression (Meistrich and Hess, 2013; Nakata et al., 2015; Oakberg, 1956).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meistrich and Hess, 2013; Nakata et al., 2015; Oakberg, 1956.

claim: Spermiogenesis is the sub-process through which post-meiotic spermatids develop into mature spermatozoa.
source: Note that the sub-process through which post-meiotic spermatids develop into mature spermatozoa is termed 'spermiogenesis' (Bao and Bedford, 2016), which is marked by a series of cellular remodeling events that include chromatin condensation, flagellum formation, elimination of redundant cytoplasm, and biogenesis of the acrosome—an acidic, membranous organelle positioned over the anterior part of the sperm nucleus that functions in fertilization of the egg (Moreno and Alvarado, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bao and Bedford, 2016 and Moreno and Alvarado, 2006.

claim: Spermiogenesis is marked by chromatin condensation, flagellum formation, elimination of redundant cytoplasm, and biogenesis of the acrosome.
source: Note that the sub-process through which post-meiotic spermatids develop into mature spermatozoa is termed 'spermiogenesis' (Bao and Bedford, 2016), which is marked by a series of cellular remodeling events that include chromatin condensation, flagellum formation, elimination of redundant cytoplasm, and biogenesis of the acrosome—an acidic, membranous organelle positioned over the anterior part of the sperm nucleus that functions in fertilization of the egg (Moreno and Alvarado, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bao and Bedford, 2016 and Moreno and Alvarado, 2006.

claim: The acrosome is an acidic, membranous organelle positioned over the anterior part of the sperm nucleus that functions in fertilization of the egg.
source: Note that the sub-process through which post-meiotic spermatids develop into mature spermatozoa is termed 'spermiogenesis' (Bao and Bedford, 2016), which is marked by a series of cellular remodeling events that include chromatin condensation, flagellum formation, elimination of redundant cytoplasm, and biogenesis of the acrosome—an acidic, membranous organelle positioned over the anterior part of the sperm nucleus that functions in fertilization of the egg (Moreno and Alvarado, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moreno and Alvarado, 2006.

claim: The transformation of round spermatids involves the cytoskeletal system, especially microfilaments.
source: The transformation of round spermatids involves the cytoskeletal system, especially microfilaments (Soda et al., 2020), which shuttles protein and vesicles to the nascent acrosome via dynamic cytoskeletal remodeling orchestrated by various accessory proteins such as the actin-binding protein PROFILIN-3 (Umer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soda et al., 2020 and Umer et al., 2021.

claim: Microfilaments shuttle protein and vesicles to the nascent acrosome via dynamic cytoskeletal remodeling orchestrated by various accessory proteins such as PROFILIN-3.
source: The transformation of round spermatids involves the cytoskeletal system, especially microfilaments (Soda et al., 2020), which shuttles protein and vesicles to the nascent acrosome via dynamic cytoskeletal remodeling orchestrated by various accessory proteins such as the actin-binding protein PROFILIN-3 (Umer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soda et al., 2020 and Umer et al., 2021.

claim: The formation of the acrosome is characterized by the generation, trafficking, and fusion of vesicles that harbor essential acrosomal components such as hydrolytic enzymes and proteases.
source: Typically, the formation of the acrosome, which is characterized by the generation, trafficking, and fusion of vesicles that harbor the essential acrosomal components such as hydrolytic enzymes and proteases involved in the acrosome reaction, occurs simultaneously with the process of 16-step spermatid differentiation (Teves et al., 2020) that has been well documented morphologically.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Teves et al., 2020.

claim: Acrosome formation occurs simultaneously with the process of 16-step spermatid differentiation.
source: Typically, the formation of the acrosome, which is characterized by the generation, trafficking, and fusion of vesicles that harbor the essential acrosomal components such as hydrolytic enzymes and proteases involved in the acrosome reaction, occurs simultaneously with the process of 16-step spermatid differentiation (Teves et al., 2020) that has been well documented morphologically.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Teves et al., 2020.

claim: Acrosome biogenesis follows four sequential phases: the Golgi phase, cap phase, acrosome phase, and maturation phase.
source: According to the classical descriptions of acrosome biogenesis that follows four sequential phases (the Golgi phase, cap phase, acrosome phase, and maturation phase) (Clermont and Leblond, 1955), the nascent acrosome is sequentially assembled from the so-called proacrosomal vesicles that originate from the Golgi apparatus through the biosynthetic pathway (Khawar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clermont and Leblond, 1955 and Khawar et al., 2019.

claim: The nascent acrosome is sequentially assembled from proacrosomal vesicles that originate from the Golgi apparatus through the biosynthetic pathway.
source: According to the classical descriptions of acrosome biogenesis that follows four sequential phases (the Golgi phase, cap phase, acrosome phase, and maturation phase) (Clermont and Leblond, 1955), the nascent acrosome is sequentially assembled from the so-called proacrosomal vesicles that originate from the Golgi apparatus through the biosynthetic pathway (Khawar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clermont and Leblond, 1955 and Khawar et al., 2019.

claim: The endocytic machinery is implicated in vesicular trafficking toward the growing acrosome.
source: However, recent experimental findings have implicated some other cellular components (e.g., the endocytic machinery) in vesicular trafficking toward the growing acrosome (Berruti and Paiardi, 2015; Li et al., 2006), supporting the existence of an extra-Golgi supply of proacrosomal vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berruti and Paiardi, 2015 and Li et al., 2006.

claim: There exists an extra-Golgi supply of proacrosomal vesicles.
source: However, recent experimental findings have implicated some other cellular components (e.g., the endocytic machinery) in vesicular trafficking toward the growing acrosome (Berruti and Paiardi, 2015; Li et al., 2006), supporting the existence of an extra-Golgi supply of proacrosomal vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berruti and Paiardi, 2015 and Li et al., 2006.

claim: F-actin functions as a cytoskeletal transport platform for proacrosomal vesicles.
source: Notably, the role of filamentous actin (F-actin) as a cytoskeletal transport platform for proacrosomal vesicles has been documented (Kierszenbaum et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kierszenbaum et al., 2003b.

claim: GOPC functions in the transport/fusion of proacrosomal vesicles.
source: In addition, several Golgi-associated proteins are known to function in the transport/fusion of proacrosomal vesicles, including Golgi-associated PDZ and coiled-coil motif-containing protein (GOPC) (Yao et al., 2002), protein interacting with C kinase 1 (PICK1) (Xiao et al., 2009), and Golgi matrix protein 130 (GM130) (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yao et al., 2002.

claim: PICK1 functions in the transport/fusion of proacrosomal vesicles.
source: In addition, several Golgi-associated proteins are known to function in the transport/fusion of proacrosomal vesicles, including Golgi-associated PDZ and coiled-coil motif-containing protein (GOPC) (Yao et al., 2002), protein interacting with C kinase 1 (PICK1) (Xiao et al., 2009), and Golgi matrix protein 130 (GM130) (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xiao et al., 2009.

claim: GM130 functions in the transport/fusion of proacrosomal vesicles.
source: In addition, several Golgi-associated proteins are known to function in the transport/fusion of proacrosomal vesicles, including Golgi-associated PDZ and coiled-coil motif-containing protein (GOPC) (Yao et al., 2002), protein interacting with C kinase 1 (PICK1) (Xiao et al., 2009), and Golgi matrix protein 130 (GM130) (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Han et al., 2017.

claim: The autophagic machinery contributes to Golgi-derived proacrosomal vesicle trafficking.
source: More recently, the contribution of the autophagic machinery in Golgi-derived proacrosomal vesicle trafficking has been identified by germ cell-specific Atg7-KO (Wang et al., 2014b) and Sirt1-KO (Liu et al., 2017) mouse models, offering new insights into the molecular mechanisms through which the acrosome develops.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2014b and Liu et al., 2017.

claim: COFILIN is an actin-binding protein known for its cutting and depolymerizing functions that promote the remodeling of actin filaments.
source: As an actin-binding protein, COFILIN is widely known for its cutting and depolymerizing functions that promote the subsequent remodeling of actin filaments (Wioland et al., 2017), which is required for many actin-driven events such as mitosis (Amano et al., 2002) and organelle trafficking (Cichon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wioland et al., 2017, Amano et al., 2002, and Cichon et al., 2012.

claim: COFILIN-mediated actin remodeling is required for mitosis.
source: As an actin-binding protein, COFILIN is widely known for its cutting and depolymerizing functions that promote the subsequent remodeling of actin filaments (Wioland et al., 2017), which is required for many actin-driven events such as mitosis (Amano et al., 2002) and organelle trafficking (Cichon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Amano et al., 2002.

claim: COFILIN-mediated actin remodeling is required for organelle trafficking.
source: As an actin-binding protein, COFILIN is widely known for its cutting and depolymerizing functions that promote the subsequent remodeling of actin filaments (Wioland et al., 2017), which is required for many actin-driven events such as mitosis (Amano et al., 2002) and organelle trafficking (Cichon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cichon et al., 2012.

claim: COFILIN can stimulate actin nucleation at a high COFILIN/actin concentration ratio, which favors actin filament assembly.
source: Intriguingly, COFILIN was also found to stimulate actin nucleation at a high COFILIN/actin concentration ratio, which in turn favors actin filament assembly (Andrianantoandro and Pollard, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Andrianantoandro and Pollard, 2006.

claim: COFILIN activity is modulated by post-translational modifications, protein binding, and redox reactions.
source: It follows that the complex modulation of COFILIN activity, consisting of post-translational modifications, protein binding, and redox reactions (Namme et al., 2021), enables the proper rearrangement of F-actin organization in response to various extracellular stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Namme et al., 2021.

claim: Phosphorylation/dephosphorylation at the Ser-3 residue is the most crucial regulatory mechanism for COFILIN activity.
source: Among these regulatory mechanisms, the phosphorylation/dephosphorylation at the Ser-3 residue stands out as the most crucial.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge based on the context of COFILIN regulation.

claim: Phosphorylation-mediated inactivation by LIMKs prevents COFILIN's actin remodeling functions.
source: Phosphorylation-mediated inactivation by LIM domain kinases (LIMKs) prevents COFILIN's actin remodeling functions (Arber et al., 1998), whereas activating dephosphorylation of COFILIN is catalyzed by phosphatases such as chronophin (Gohla et al., 2005) and the Slingshot (SSH) family of proteins (Niwa et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arber et al., 1998, Gohla et al., 2005, and Niwa et al., 2002.

claim: Activating dephosphorylation of COFILIN is catalyzed by chronophin.
source: Phosphorylation-mediated inactivation by LIM domain kinases (LIMKs) prevents COFILIN's actin remodeling functions (Arber et al., 1998), whereas activating dephosphorylation of COFILIN is catalyzed by phosphatases such as chronophin (Gohla et al., 2005) and the Slingshot (SSH) family of proteins (Niwa et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gohla et al., 2005.

claim: Activating dephosphorylation of COFILIN is catalyzed by the Slingshot (SSH) family of proteins.
source: Phosphorylation-mediated inactivation by LIM domain kinases (LIMKs) prevents COFILIN's actin remodeling functions (Arber et al., 1998), whereas activating dephosphorylation of COFILIN is catalyzed by phosphatases such as chronophin (Gohla et al., 2005) and the Slingshot (SSH) family of proteins (Niwa et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Niwa et al., 2002.

claim: Cofilin phospho-regulation is involved in cell movement.
source: Several studies have reported the cofilin phospho-regulation of diverse cellular processes including cell movement (Nishita et al., 2005), cytokinesis (Kaji et al., 2003), and germ cell development (Takahashi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nishita et al., 2005.

claim: Cofilin phospho-regulation is involved in cytokinesis.
source: Several studies have reported the cofilin phospho-regulation of diverse cellular processes including cell movement (Nishita et al., 2005), cytokinesis (Kaji et al., 2003), and germ cell development (Takahashi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kaji et al., 2003.

claim: Cofilin phospho-regulation is involved in germ cell development.
source: Several studies have reported the cofilin phospho-regulation of diverse cellular processes including cell movement (Nishita et al., 2005), cytokinesis (Kaji et al., 2003), and germ cell development (Takahashi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Takahashi et al., 2002.

claim: The ssh gene was originally identified in Drosophila mutants with the bifurcation phenotype of bristles and hairs.
source: The ssh gene was originally identified in Drosophila mutants with the bifurcation phenotype of bristles and hairs (Niwa et al., 2002), and the mammalian homologs encode a set of COFILIN phosphatases, namely the SSH phosphatases.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Niwa et al., 2002.

claim: SSH1 is the most well-characterized isoform of SSH phosphatases.
source: Some biological relevance of SSHs has been revealed, especially the most well-characterized isoform SSH1 (Bielig et al., 2014), while much less is known about SSH2 other than its role as a regulator of actin remodeling during neutrophil chemotaxis (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bielig et al., 2014.

claim: SSH2 functions as a regulator of actin remodeling during neutrophil chemotaxis.
source: Some biological relevance of SSHs has been revealed, especially the most well-characterized isoform SSH1 (Bielig et al., 2014), while much less is known about SSH2 other than its role as a regulator of actin remodeling during neutrophil chemotaxis (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2015.

claim: SSH2 exhibits relatively higher expression in testes compared to other organs in mice.
source: According to a gene-expression study focusing on the SSHs, relatively higher expression of SSH2 was observed in testes compared to other organs in mice (Ohta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ohta et al., 2003.

claim: SSH2 exhibited increasing protein abundance changes with the proceeding of murine spermatogenesis.
source: Moreover, in the light of a recent proteomic study which is aiming at the prediction of meiosis-essential genes, SSH2 exhibited increasing protein abundance changes with the proceeding of murine spermatogenesis (Fang et al., 2021), illustrating its potential role in male germ cell development.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fang et al., 2021.

claim: SSH2 is an activator of COFILIN-mediated actin cytoskeleton remodeling.
source: By generating mice carrying targeted knockout (KO) of Ssh2 and knock-in (KI) mice expressing hemagglutinin (HA)-tagged SSH2, we found that SSH2 is an activator of COFILIN-mediated actin cytoskeleton remodeling and is essential for proper acrosome biogenesis during spermatogenesis and thus required for male fertility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Ssh2 KO and KI mice.

claim: SSH2 is essential for proper acrosome biogenesis during spermatogenesis.
source: By generating mice carrying targeted knockout (KO) of Ssh2 and knock-in (KI) mice expressing hemagglutinin (HA)-tagged SSH2, we found that SSH2 is an activator of COFILIN-mediated actin cytoskeleton remodeling and is essential for proper acrosome biogenesis during spermatogenesis and thus required for male fertility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Ssh2 KO and KI mice.

claim: The impaired acrosome biogenesis in Ssh2 KO mice is likely a consequence of abnormal vesicular trafficking/fusion that can be attributed to disrupted F-actin remodeling.
source: The impaired acrosome biogenesis in Ssh2 KO mice is likely a consequence of abnormal vesicular trafficking/fusion that can be attributed to disrupted F-actin remodeling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations in the study.

claim: Ssh2 KO mice were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing with deletion of exon 8.
source: To explore the role of SSH2 in male fertility, we generated mice with Ssh2 KO lacking exon 8 using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental methods described and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SSH2 protein was absent in Ssh2 KO testicular samples.
source: We confirmed the Ssh2 KO status in mice using PCR of tail-derived genomic DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and western blotting (WB) of whole testicular lysates. SSH2 was immunodetected in the testes of wild-type (WT) mice but was absent in the Ssh2 KO samples (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ssh2 KO male mice were found to be completely infertile.
source: Regarding reproductive functional activity, Ssh2 KO male mice were found to be completely infertile (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by fertility test data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No pups were obtained when adult Ssh2 KO males were mated with WT fertile females.
source: Six mice of each genotype were examined for fertility test for 2 months. The data indicated infertile status as no pups were obtained when adult Ssh2 KO males were mated with WT fertile females (8 weeks of age).
evidence: This is supported by fertility test data.

claim: There were no differences in testis size, body weight, testis weight, or testis-to-body weight ratio in Ssh2 KO male mice compared to WT littermates.
source: We examined no differences in the size of the testis, body weight, testis weight, or testis-to-body weight ratio in Ssh2 KO male mice compared to their WT littermates (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1D-G.

claim: No elongating or elongated spermatids were detected in Ssh2 KO testes.
source: Histology of the testis and cauda epididymis from WT and Ssh2 KO mice. Sections were stained with hematoxylin. No elongating or elongated spermatids were detected in Ssh2 KO testes, and no mature sperm were detected in the Ssh2 KO epididymis.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: No mature sperm were detected in the Ssh2 KO epididymis.
source: Histology of the testis and cauda epididymis from WT and Ssh2 KO mice. Sections were stained with hematoxylin. No elongating or elongated spermatids were detected in Ssh2 KO testes, and no mature sperm were detected in the Ssh2 KO epididymis.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Total sperm number in the cauda epididymis of Ssh2 KO mice was zero.
source: (I) Total sperm number in the cauda epididymis of WT (11.92×106 ± 0.82×106) and Ssh2 KO (0.00) mice, n=6.
evidence: This is supported by sperm count data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Almost no elongating or elongated spermatids were observed in the testes of Ssh2 KO males.
source: The seminiferous tubules of WT testes were full of spermatogenic cells and contained a basal population of spermatogonia, spermatocytes, and spermatids. In contrast, almost no elongating or elongated spermatids were observed in the testes of Ssh2 KO males; instead, round spermatid aggregates were found to form a giant multinucleated cell that were further verified to be spermatid clusters by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) assessment (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and FACS data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Round spermatid aggregates in Ssh2 KO testes form giant multinucleated cells.
source: The seminiferous tubules of WT testes were full of spermatogenic cells and contained a basal population of spermatogonia, spermatocytes, and spermatids. In contrast, almost no elongating or elongated spermatids were observed in the testes of Ssh2 KO males; instead, round spermatid aggregates were found to form a giant multinucleated cell that were further verified to be spermatid clusters by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) assessment (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and FACS data.

claim: The prophase I process was successfully completed in WT and Ssh2 KO mice.
source: By immunofluorescence co-staining of synaptonemal complex protein 1 (SYCP1) and SYCP3 in the nuclei of spermatocyte spreads—which comprise the central and lateral elements of the synaptonemal complex, respectively (de Vries et al., 2005; Yuan et al., 2000)—we found no obvious differences in their distribution patterns in various stages of meiotic prophase, indicating that the prophase I process was successfully completed in WT and Ssh2 KO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Testes collected from Ssh2 KO mice at PD7 and PD14 were indistinguishable from those of WT mice.
source: Testes collected from Ssh2 KO mice at postnatal day (PD)7 and PD14 were indistinguishable from those of WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Round spermatid clusters were first observed in Ssh2 KO tubules at PD28.
source: The most advanced cells in WT testes were elongating spermatids at PD28, and none of these were present in Ssh2 KO testes. Round spermatid clusters were first observed in Ssh2 KO tubules at PD28, and these accumulated from PD35 to PD60.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis.

claim: Spermatogenesis of Ssh2 KO mice was arrested at stages II-III.
source: To determine the developmental defects at specific stages of spermatogenesis, tissue sections of WT and Ssh2 KO testes were stained with hematoxylin and periodic acid Schiff (PAS) and then labeled with acrosomal glycoproteins. We found that spermatogenesis of Ssh2 KO mice was arrested at stages Ⅱ-Ⅲ (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by PAS-hematoxylin staining shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only step 1-3 round spermatids were present in Ssh2 KO tubules.
source: Spermatids at various steps of spermiogenesis were observed in WT seminiferous tubules, whereas only step 1–3 round spermatids were present in Ssh2 KO tubules, indicating spermiogenic failure in these mice.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis.

claim: Round spermatids with malformed acrosomal structures were detected in Ssh2 KO testes.
source: We also detected round spermatids with malformed acrosomal structures in Ssh2 KO testes, which suggests that the acrosomal formation was also affected.
evidence: This is supported by histological observations.

claim: Clustered round spermatids and apoptotic-like germ cells were observed in Ssh2 KO mice tubules.
source: Furthermore, clustered round spermatids and apoptotic-like germ cells were also observed in Ssh2 KO mice tubules exhibiting small hyperchromatic nuclei and polynuclear structures, which are known indicator of apoptosis (Catalano-Iniesta et al., 2019; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 2A and citation to Catalano-Iniesta et al., 2019.

claim: The counts of TUNEL-positive cells were significantly increased in the Ssh2 KO seminiferous tubules.
source: We performed a terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase-dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) assay to identify the apoptotic cells in the testes and epididymides of WT and Ssh2 KO mice. The counts of TUNEL-positive cells were significantly increased in the Ssh2 KO seminiferous tubules which were observed primarily as apoptotic spermatids, as indicated by the nuclear morphology and location within spermatogenic epithelium (Figure 2B, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Large numbers of isolated apoptotic spermatids were found in the lumen of epididymal ducts of Ssh2 KO mice.
source: Similarly, we found large numbers of isolated apoptotic spermatids in the lumen of epididymal ducts of Ssh2 KO mice (Figure 2B, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: Elevated protein levels of pro-apoptotic BAX, BAD, Caspase-3, and cleaved Caspase-3 were detected in the testicular lysates of Ssh2 KO mice.
source: As demonstrated by WB, in comparison with that of WT mice, remarkably elevated protein levels of pro-apoptotic BAX, BAD, Caspase-3, and cleaved Caspase-3 accompanied by relatively decreased protein levels of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins were detected in the testicular lysates of Ssh2 KO mice (Figure 2E), suggesting the induction of Caspase-3 activation in the spermatogenic cell apoptosis resulted from Ssh2 KO.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Relatively decreased protein levels of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 were detected in the testicular lysates of Ssh2 KO mice.
source: As demonstrated by WB, in comparison with that of WT mice, remarkably elevated protein levels of pro-apoptotic BAX, BAD, Caspase-3, and cleaved Caspase-3 accompanied by relatively decreased protein levels of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins were detected in the testicular lysates of Ssh2 KO mice (Figure 2E), suggesting the induction of Caspase-3 activation in the spermatogenic cell apoptosis resulted from Ssh2 KO.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Ssh2 KO results in spermatid apoptosis via the Bcl-2/Caspase-3 signaling pathway.
source: Consistently, these findings support the hypothesis that Ssh2 KO resultant round spermatid arrest with malformed acrosomes during spermatogenesis and that ultimately causes spermatid apoptosis via the Bcl-2/Caspase-3 signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of apoptotic markers.

claim: Multiple scattered proacrosomic vesicles separated from nuclei were present in a majority of the Ssh2 KO spermatids.
source: On the contrary, instead of intact acrosomal vesicles as seen in WT spermatids, multiple scattered proacrosomic vesicles separated from nuclei (without fusing with each other) were present in a majority of the Ssh2 KO spermatids (steps 1–3) (Figure 3A, lower panel), demonstrating that acrosome biogenesis was disrupted starting from the Golgi phase in Ssh2 KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Acrosome biogenesis was disrupted starting from the Golgi phase in Ssh2 KO mice.
source: On the contrary, instead of intact acrosomal vesicles as seen in WT spermatids, multiple scattered proacrosomic vesicles separated from nuclei (without fusing with each other) were present in a majority of the Ssh2 KO spermatids (steps 1–3) (Figure 3A, lower panel), demonstrating that acrosome biogenesis was disrupted starting from the Golgi phase in Ssh2 KO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from immunofluorescence observations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In Ssh2 KO spermatids, multiple Golgi-derived small proacrosomal vesicles were adjacent to the trans-face of the Golgi apparatus and failed to fuse together.
source: TEM showed that WT spermatids had a single, large acrosomal vesicle in which the granule was attached to the concave surface of the nucleus and the inner acrosomal membrane was docked to the electron-dense acroplaxome. However, in Ssh2 KO spermatids, multiple Golgi-derived small proacrosomal vesicles were adjacent to the trans-face of the Golgi apparatus which contain thick Golgi stacks and failed to fuse together to yield the acrosomal vesicle.
evidence: This is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No acroplaxome-like structure was observed near the nuclear envelope in Ssh2 KO spermatids.
source: Moreover, no acroplaxome-like structure was observed near the nuclear envelope (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The impairment of acrosomal formation in Ssh2 KO mice might be due to the failure of proacrosomal vesicle fusion and/or defects in vesicular trafficking toward the nuclear surface.
source: These results suggest that the impairment of acrosomal formation in Ssh2 KO mice might be due to the failure of proacrosomal vesicle fusion and/or defects in vesicular trafficking toward the nuclear surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from TEM observations.

claim: GM130 is known to function in Golgi membrane dynamics and fusion of Golgi-derived vesicles.
source: Notably, such impaired acrosome biogenesis phenotype appears similar to observations in mice with mutations in Gm130 (Han et al., 2017), which is known to function in Golgi membrane dynamics and fusion of Golgi-derived vesicles (Koreishi et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Han et al., 2017, Koreishi et al., 2013, and Walker et al., 2004.

claim: In Ssh2 KO spermatids, only large GM130-positive fluorescent aggregates that exhibited no association with PNA-positive proacrosomal vesicles were observed.
source: We observed GM130 signals with vesicle-like and stack-like shapes in close contact with the PNA-labeled acrosomal vesicles in WT spermatids. However, in Ssh2 KO spermatids, only large GM130-positive fluorescent aggregates that exhibited no association with PNA-positive proacrosomal vesicles were observed (Figure 3C), suggesting that the localization of vesicular fusion-associated GM130 is altered in Golgi-phase spermatids by Ssh2 KO.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The localization of vesicular fusion-associated GM130 is altered in Golgi-phase spermatids by Ssh2 KO.
source: We observed GM130 signals with vesicle-like and stack-like shapes in close contact with the PNA-labeled acrosomal vesicles in WT spermatids. However, in Ssh2 KO spermatids, only large GM130-positive fluorescent aggregates that exhibited no association with PNA-positive proacrosomal vesicles were observed (Figure 3C), suggesting that the localization of vesicular fusion-associated GM130 is altered in Golgi-phase spermatids by Ssh2 KO.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from immunofluorescence observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ssh2 KO causes failure of proacrosomal vesicle fusion.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that Ssh2 KO causes failure of proacrosomal vesicle fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: SSH2 protein was undetectable in PD7 testes, became detectable at PD14, and substantially increased by PD21.
source: We observed a gradual increase in accumulation during murine spermatogenesis. The protein was undetectable in PD7 testes, became detectable at PD14, and substantially the level was increased by PD21, the time when round spermatids first appear in seminiferous tubules (Guan et al., 2020), suggesting a potential function of SSH2 in the development of spermatid (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Round spermatids first appear in seminiferous tubules at PD21.
source: We observed a gradual increase in accumulation during murine spermatogenesis. The protein was undetectable in PD7 testes, became detectable at PD14, and substantially the level was increased by PD21, the time when round spermatids first appear in seminiferous tubules (Guan et al., 2020), suggesting a potential function of SSH2 in the development of spermatid (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guan et al., 2020.

claim: SSH2 has a potential function in the development of spermatid.
source: We observed a gradual increase in accumulation during murine spermatogenesis. The protein was undetectable in PD7 testes, became detectable at PD14, and substantially the level was increased by PD21, the time when round spermatids first appear in seminiferous tubules (Guan et al., 2020), suggesting a potential function of SSH2 in the development of spermatid (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal expression pattern of SSH2 shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SSH2 accumulated predominantly in spermatocytes and post-meiotic round spermatids.
source: To determine the developmental roles of SSH2 in spermatogenic cells, we performed counterstaining of SSH2 with PNA on seminiferous tubule paraffin sections of WT and Ssh2 KO mice. SSH2 accumulated predominantly in spermatocytes and post-meiotic round spermatids.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: Bright, isolated SSH2-positive puncta were positioned in the acrosomal region next to the nuclei of round spermatids.
source: In addition to the ubiquitous distribution observed in the cytoplasm of the germ cells, we noted bright, isolated SSH2-positive puncta positioned in the acrosomal region next to the nuclei of round spermatids (Figure 4B, left column).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Fragmented acrosomes with a lack of SSH2 signal were detected in Ssh2 KO spermatids.
source: In contrast, fragmented acrosomes with a lack of SSH2 signal were detected in Ssh2 KO spermatids (Figure 4B, right column).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The association of SSH2 with the growing acrosome was evident by the acrosomal localization of SSH2 in the spermatids of WT mice.
source: Moreover, the association of SSH2 with the growing acrosome was evident by the acrosomal localization of SSH2 in the spermatids of WT mice (Figure 4C, upper panels) which was further confirmed by the distribution of HA-tagged SSH2 (SSH2-HA) detected on the testicular sections of the CRISPR/Cas9-generated viable mice harboring an HA-epitope fusion variant of SSH2.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SSH2-HA is predominantly localized in the cytoplasm of spermatocytes and round spermatids with an intensive accumulation at the acrosomal region.
source: Immunofluorescence staining against the HA-tag showed that SSH2-HA is predominantly localized in the cytoplasm of spermatocytes and round spermatids with an intensive accumulation at the acrosomal region, consistent with the observations of the endogenous SSH2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Punctate PNA signals representing the nascent acrosome surrounded with robust SSH2-HA fluorescence signals were detected in Golgi-phase round spermatids.
source: Notably, punctate PNA signals which represent the nascent acrosome surrounded with robust SSH2-HA fluorescence signals were detected in Golgi-phase round spermatids within stage Ⅰ-Ⅲ tubules, instead of prevalent acrosomal localization of SSH2-HA in round spermatids at the cap phase of acrosome biogenesis, implying diverse roles of SSH2 in this continuous process (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SSH2 has diverse roles in the continuous process of acrosome biogenesis.
source: Notably, punctate PNA signals which represent the nascent acrosome surrounded with robust SSH2-HA fluorescence signals were detected in Golgi-phase round spermatids within stage Ⅰ-Ⅲ tubules, instead of prevalent acrosomal localization of SSH2-HA in round spermatids at the cap phase of acrosome biogenesis, implying diverse roles of SSH2 in this continuous process (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the different localization patterns of SSH2-HA at different phases shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SSH2 is functionally involved in acrosome biogenesis.
source: Together, these results show that SSH2 is functionally involved in acrosome biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the localization and expression studies.

claim: SSH2 binds to F-actin in cultured HeLa cells.
source: It has been reported that SSH2 binds to F-actin in cultured HeLa cells, where it antagonizes LIMK1-induced actin polymerization (Ohta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ohta et al., 2003.

claim: SSH2 antagonizes LIMK1-induced actin polymerization in cultured HeLa cells.
source: It has been reported that SSH2 binds to F-actin in cultured HeLa cells, where it antagonizes LIMK1-induced actin polymerization (Ohta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ohta et al., 2003.

claim: F-actin staining was altered in Ssh2 KO spermatids.
source: As the representative images showed, the F-actin staining was altered in Ssh2 KO spermatids. Unlike the expected sharp, sickle-shape heads of elongated spermatids surrounded by organized F-actin bundles seen in WT mice, the F-actin aggregated to form numerous lumps in Ssh2 KO round spermatids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phalloidin staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: F-actin aggregated to form numerous lumps in Ssh2 KO round spermatids.
source: As the representative images showed, the F-actin staining was altered in Ssh2 KO spermatids. Unlike the expected sharp, sickle-shape heads of elongated spermatids surrounded by organized F-actin bundles seen in WT mice, the F-actin aggregated to form numerous lumps in Ssh2 KO round spermatids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phalloidin staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of Ssh2 accelerates filament growth in spermatids rather than inducing filament disassembly.
source: This aberrant accumulation of F-actin suggests that loss of Ssh2 accelerates filament growth in spermatids rather than inducing filament disassembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the F-actin staining observations.

claim: Punctate phalloidin signals accompanied by thick F-actin bundles were mostly dissociated from the fractured acrosomes in Ssh2 KO spermatids.
source: Phalloidin staining was diffusely distributed in the cytoplasm of round spermatids and intact F-actin bundles that were located around the laminal acrosomes in elongated spermatids of WT mice. In contrast, punctate phalloidin signals accompanied by thick F-actin bundles were mostly dissociated from the fractured acrosomes in Ssh2 KO spermatids (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Robust phalloidin staining was scattered irregularly in Ssh2 KO spermatids and exhibited no association with the acrosomal signals.
source: Moreover, we co-immunostained the spermatids with phalloidin and PNA in seminiferous tubule squashes from WT and Ssh2 KO mice. As expected, confocal microscopy showed that punctate F-actin signals were distributed ubiquitously throughout the cytoplasm of Golgi-phase spermatids of WT mice, with relatively intense fluorescence signals localized at acrosomal regions. However, robust phalloidin staining was scattered irregularly in Ssh2 KO spermatids and exhibited no association with the acrosomal signals (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: F-actin is highly disorganized in Ssh2 KO spermatids during acrosome biogenesis.
source: Together, these findings indicate that F-actin is highly disorganized in Ssh2 KO spermatids during acrosome biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the F-actin staining observations.

claim: SSH2 facilitates Golgi-acrosome vesicular trafficking by modulating F-actin organization.
source: Given the disrupted acrosome biogenesis and disorganized F-actin in Ssh2 KO spermatids, we hypothesized that SSH2 facilitates Golgi-acrosome vesicular trafficking by modulating F-actin organization.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental observations.

claim: In WT Golgi-phase spermatids, GOPC retained its distinct distribution predominantly confined to the acrosomal region as indicated by its colocalization with PNA-positive structures.
source: In WT Golgi-phase spermatids, GOPC retained its distinct distribution, which was predominantly confined to the acrosomal region as indicated by its colocalization with PNA-positive structures near the nuclei (76.50 ± 3.70%).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: In Ssh2 KO spermatids, GOPC exhibited dispersed localization in the cytoplasm and the extent of GOPC-PNA colocalization was significantly diminished.
source: In contrast, in Ssh2 KO spermatids GOPC exhibited dispersed localization in the cytoplasm and the extent of GOPC-PNA colocalization was significantly diminished (23.75 ± 7.72%) (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The participation of GOPC in proacrosomal vesicle trafficking is negatively affected in Ssh2 KO mice.
source: These results suggest that the participation of GOPC in proacrosomal vesicle trafficking is negatively affected in Ssh2 KO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the GOPC localization observations.

claim: LC3 was localized on proacrosomal vesicles in most of the WT spermatids (89.45 ± 2.50%).
source: We observed that LC3 was localized on proacrosomal vesicles in most of the WT spermatids (89.45 ± 2.50%), as indicated by its colocalization with PNA.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: A portion of the LC3 molecules was not recruited to proacrosome vesicles in Ssh2 KO spermatids (77.75 ± 5.91%).
source: In contrast, vesicle-like LC3-positive fluorescent signals surrounded the PNA-positive structures, and a portion of the LC3 molecules was not recruited to proacrosome vesicles in Ssh2 KO spermatids (77.75 ± 5.91%) (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: Ssh2 KO results in impaired trafficking of proacrosomal vesicles to the growing acrosome.
source: Together, these results indicate that Ssh2 KO results in impaired trafficking of proacrosomal vesicles to the growing acrosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GOPC and LC3 localization studies.

claim: The Ssh2 KO mice had elevated levels of p-COFILIN compared to their WT littermates.
source: To pursue this further, we monitored the expression of COFILIN, phospho-COFILIN (p-COFILIN), and protein kinases that directly phosphorylate COFILIN (e.g., LIMK1 and LIMK2; Arber et al., 1998) by WB of testicular lysates of PD82 WT and Ssh2 KO testes. The Ssh2 KO mice had elevated levels of p-COFILIN compared to their WT littermates, whereas there were no significant differences in the levels of total COFILIN, LIMK1, or LIMK2 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There were no significant differences in the levels of total COFILIN, LIMK1, or LIMK2 between Ssh2 KO and WT mice.
source: To pursue this further, we monitored the expression of COFILIN, phospho-COFILIN (p-COFILIN), and protein kinases that directly phosphorylate COFILIN (e.g., LIMK1 and LIMK2; Arber et al., 1998) by WB of testicular lysates of PD82 WT and Ssh2 KO testes. The Ssh2 KO mice had elevated levels of p-COFILIN compared to their WT littermates, whereas there were no significant differences in the levels of total COFILIN, LIMK1, or LIMK2 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The signal intensity of p-COFILIN was dramatically increased in both the nucleus and cytoplasm of Ssh2 KO spermatogenic cells, specifically in spermatids.
source: Accordingly, we also conducted an immunofluorescent analysis on testicular sections from adult WT and Ssh2 KO mice using the antibody against p-COFILIN. Notwithstanding some mild nuclear staining in round spermatids, we did not observe evident p-COFILIN signals in the germ cells in WT testes. As expected, compared to WT mice, the signal intensity of p-COFILIN was dramatically increased in both the nucleus and cytoplasm of Ssh2 KO spermatogenic cells, specifically in spermatids (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: COFILIN phospho-regulation is impaired in Ssh2 KO testes with subsequent accumulation of p-COFILIN.
source: These findings suggest that COFILIN phospho-regulation is impaired in Ssh2 KO testes with subsequent accumulation of p-COFILIN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the p-COFILIN expression studies.

claim: Increased expression of F-actin accompanied by p-COFILIN was observed in Ssh2 KO testes.
source: To further determine whether the effect of SSH2 on the actin cytoskeleton is mediated by the control of COFILIN phospho-regulation, we performed both WB and immunostaining against SSH2, p-COFILIN, and F-ACTIN in WT and Ssh2 KO testicular lysates and sections, respectively. Not surprisingly, we observed increased expression of F-actin accompanied by p-COFILIN in Ssh2 KO testes (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Ubiquitous p-COFILIN signals overlapping with disorganized F-actin aggregates were observed in Ssh2 KO spermatids.
source: Fluorescence images also showed ubiquitous p-COFILIN signals overlapping with disorganized F-actin aggregates in Ssh2 KO spermatids (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: SSH2 orchestrates F-actin remodeling through the control of COFILIN phosphorylation during acrosome biogenesis.
source: Collectively, these findings support a role for SSH2 in orchestrating F-actin remodeling through the control of COFILIN phosphorylation during acrosome biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of p-COFILIN and F-actin.

claim: The organ distribution of SSH family members varies significantly in mice.
source: Although SSHs exert COFILIN phosphatase activity in mammals, the organ distribution of SSH family members varies significantly in mice, implying their similar but diverse biochemical functions (Ohta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ohta et al., 2003.

claim: The males lacking functional SSH2 display disrupted germ cell development starting from the spermiogenic step 2-3 round spermatids.
source: The males lacking functional SSH2 display disrupted germ cell development starting from the spermiogenic step 2–3 round spermatids.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Embryonic lethality occurs in Cofilin-1 KO mice.
source: The implication of COFILIN during reproductive developmental process has been described in model animals, as evidenced by the embryonic lethality of Cofilin-1 KO mice (Gurniak et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gurniak et al., 2005.

claim: Non-muscle COFILIN was identified as a component of tubulobulbar complexes in rat Sertoli cells.
source: Non-muscle COFILIN was identified as a component of tubulobulbar complexes in rat Sertoli cells (Guttman et al., 2004) and as a key activator of human sperm capacitation and the acrosome reaction (Megnagi et al., 2015), but its functions in mammalian spermatogenesis have remained largely elusive.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guttman et al., 2004.

claim: Non-muscle COFILIN is a key activator of human sperm capacitation and the acrosome reaction.
source: Non-muscle COFILIN was identified as a component of tubulobulbar complexes in rat Sertoli cells (Guttman et al., 2004) and as a key activator of human sperm capacitation and the acrosome reaction (Megnagi et al., 2015), but its functions in mammalian spermatogenesis have remained largely elusive.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Megnagi et al., 2015.

claim: The findings of increased apoptotic index in Ssh2 KO testes are consistent with the data of abnormal testes phenotype in mice with Limk2 KO.
source: Our findings of increased apoptotic index in Ssh2 KO testes are consistent with the data of abnormal testes phenotype in mice with Limk2 KO (Takahashi et al., 2002), suggesting a potential role for COFILIN in regulating the germ cell cycle in mice.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Takahashi et al., 2002.

claim: COFILIN has a potential role in regulating the germ cell cycle in mice.
source: Our findings of increased apoptotic index in Ssh2 KO testes are consistent with the data of abnormal testes phenotype in mice with Limk2 KO (Takahashi et al., 2002), suggesting a potential role for COFILIN in regulating the germ cell cycle in mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with Limk2 KO mice.

claim: Treating A549 cells with thapsigargin induces apoptosis through the inhibition of COFILIN-mediated F-actin reorganization.
source: Another line of evidence linking COFILIN to apoptosis comes from the investigations performed in cell context. Treating A549 cells with thapsigargin, an inhibitor of endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase, also induces apoptosis through the inhibition of COFILIN-mediated F-actin reorganization (Wang et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2014a.

claim: Elevated COFILIN phosphorylation after SSH2 knockdown induces the activation of Caspase-3/7 in a human renal cell carcinoma cell line.
source: Elevated COFILIN phosphorylation after SSH2 knockdown was previously demonstrated to induce the activation of Caspase-3/7 in a human renal cell carcinoma cell line (Lu et al., 2014), and activation of Caspase-3/7 is known to trigger apoptotic cell death (Saller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lu et al., 2014 and Saller et al., 2010.

claim: Activation of Caspase-3/7 is known to trigger apoptotic cell death.
source: Elevated COFILIN phosphorylation after SSH2 knockdown was previously demonstrated to induce the activation of Caspase-3/7 in a human renal cell carcinoma cell line (Lu et al., 2014), and activation of Caspase-3/7 is known to trigger apoptotic cell death (Saller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saller et al., 2010.

claim: The mutant spermatids in Ssh2 KO mice possibly undergo cell cycle arrest via the Bcl-2/Caspase cascade due to impaired COFILIN phosphorylation.
source: Based on data from previous reports and comparing it with our findings, we speculate that the mutant spermatids in Ssh2 KO mice possibly undergo cell cycle arrest via the Bcl-2/Caspase cascade due to impaired COFILIN phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental observations and literature.

claim: The acroplaxome is a cytoskeletal actin-rich scaffold plate that anchors the acrosome to the nuclear envelope.
source: However, the observation from TEM that the lack of the electron-dense acroplaxome, a cytoskeletal actin-rich scaffold plate that anchors the acrosome to the nuclear envelope (Kierszenbaum et al., 2003a), in Ssh2 KO spermatids indicates a potential role of SSH2 in the shaping of the acroplaxome.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kierszenbaum et al., 2003a.

claim: SSH2 has a potential role in the shaping of the acroplaxome.
source: However, the observation from TEM that the lack of the electron-dense acroplaxome, a cytoskeletal actin-rich scaffold plate that anchors the acrosome to the nuclear envelope (Kierszenbaum et al., 2003a), in Ssh2 KO spermatids indicates a potential role of SSH2 in the shaping of the acroplaxome.
evidence: This is inferred from the TEM observations.

claim: Defective acroplaxome structures with impaired acrosome biogenesis were observed in mutant spermatids lacking homeodomain-interacting protein kinase 4.
source: Notably, defective acroplaxome structures with impaired acrosome biogenesis were observed in mutant spermatids lacking homeodomain-interacting protein kinase 4 (Crapster et al., 2020), which is responsible for the regulation of F-actin remodeling during spermiogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Crapster et al., 2020.

claim: Homeodomain-interacting protein kinase 4 is responsible for the regulation of F-actin remodeling during spermiogenesis.
source: Notably, defective acroplaxome structures with impaired acrosome biogenesis were observed in mutant spermatids lacking homeodomain-interacting protein kinase 4 (Crapster et al., 2020), which is responsible for the regulation of F-actin remodeling during spermiogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Crapster et al., 2020.

claim: Acrosome biogenesis in Ssh2 KO mice might be affected by the acroplaxome defects that result from disordered F-actin remodeling.
source: We infer from these findings that acrosome biogenesis in Ssh2 KO mice might also be affected by the acroplaxome defects that result from disordered F-actin remodeling, and further experiments should be performed to confirm this.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observations and literature.

claim: SSH2 might interact with MYH9, MYO19, and MYO18A.
source: According to some publicly accessible databases as the indicators of potential protein-protein interactions such as BioGRID (Oughtred et al., 2019) and IntAct (Del Toro et al., 2022), SSH2 might interact with a set of actin-based molecular motors covering MYH9, MYO19, and MYO18A, which have been implicated in the maintenance of Golgi morphology and Golgi anterograde vesicular trafficking via the PI4P/GOLPH3/MYO18A/F-actin pathway (Rahajeng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on database predictions cited from Oughtred et al., 2019 and Del Toro et al., 2022.

claim: MYH9, MYO19, and MYO18A have been implicated in the maintenance of Golgi morphology and Golgi anterograde vesicular trafficking via the PI4P/GOLPH3/MYO18A/F-actin pathway.
source: According to some publicly accessible databases as the indicators of potential protein-protein interactions such as BioGRID (Oughtred et al., 2019) and IntAct (Del Toro et al., 2022), SSH2 might interact with a set of actin-based molecular motors covering MYH9, MYO19, and MYO18A, which have been implicated in the maintenance of Golgi morphology and Golgi anterograde vesicular trafficking via the PI4P/GOLPH3/MYO18A/F-actin pathway (Rahajeng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rahajeng et al., 2019.

claim: The phenotypes of Ssh2 KO mice share similarities with that of Pick1 KO model such as acrosome fragmentation and enhanced germ cell apoptosis.
source: Moreover, it is intriguing to note that the phenotypes of Ssh2 KO mice share a lot of similarities with that of Pick1 KO model (Xiao et al., 2009) such as acrosome fragmentation and enhanced germ cell apoptosis, suggesting the possibility that SSH2 and PICK1 work together in the same trafficking machinery functioning in acrosome biogenesis which needs to be clarified further.
evidence: This is based on comparison with Pick1 KO model cited from Xiao et al., 2009.

claim: SSH2 and PICK1 might work together in the same trafficking machinery functioning in acrosome biogenesis.
source: Moreover, it is intriguing to note that the phenotypes of Ssh2 KO mice share a lot of similarities with that of Pick1 KO model (Xiao et al., 2009) such as acrosome fragmentation and enhanced germ cell apoptosis, suggesting the possibility that SSH2 and PICK1 work together in the same trafficking machinery functioning in acrosome biogenesis which needs to be clarified further.
evidence: This is a speculation based on phenotypic similarities.

claim: The Slingshot family is evolutionarily conserved in mammals.
source: In conclusion, our study confirms the requirement for SSH2 during mammalian spermatogenesis, specifically in acrosomal biogenesis. The Slingshot family is evolutionarily conserved in mammals, therefore we believe that some mutations in the SSH2 gene should exist in non-obstructive azoospermia, although no report was published yet that highlighting such mutation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Some mutations in the SSH2 gene should exist in non-obstructive azoospermia.
source: In conclusion, our study confirms the requirement for SSH2 during mammalian spermatogenesis, specifically in acrosomal biogenesis. The Slingshot family is evolutionarily conserved in mammals, therefore we believe that some mutations in the SSH2 gene should exist in non-obstructive azoospermia, although no report was published yet that highlighting such mutation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the evolutionary conservation and mouse model findings.

claim: The abnormal phenotype of Ssh2 KO in the mouse model may be valuable to understand the pathological factors causing azoospermia in humans.
source: The abnormal phenotype Ssh2 KO in the mouse model may be valuable to understand the pathological factors causing azoospermia in humans.
evidence: This is a speculation about the translational value of the findings.
